USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the newly effective Section 301 posture (25% on the $50B lists and 10% on List 3) and reopen talks without adding the threatened ~$267B tranche or locking in the January 1, 2019 jump to 25% as automatic. Use that scheduled hike as leverage, not an immediate next shot. Invite a Liu He / working-level channel and keep a possible Trump–Xi meeting on the G20 sidelines as the political off-ramp, while refusing any purchase-only truce that leaves IP and tech-transfer practices untouched.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild U.S. opportunity, not a high-cost crisis. Three days after List 3 took effect (~$250B of Chinese imports now covered) the U.S. macro tape is still strong: Michigan sentiment 100.1, industrial production 104.1, VIX ~12.9, and no recession signal. China is the more strained party—yuan ~6.88 vs ~6.28 in early April (~9.5% depreciation), industrial production growth easing to 5.8% y/y, and reserves slipping—so current U.S. tariffs retain leverage on the original Section 301 IP/tech-transfer complaint. That is why the score sits below zero rather than at neutrality. It is only a mild opportunity because the costs are real and already visible: U.S. goods exports to China are down ~7% over the window, China has matched with 5–10% tariffs on ~$60B and earlier 25% hits on soy/autos/aircraft, soybean prices have fallen from ~$11 to under $9 with new Chinese buying largely halted, and the goods deficit has widened as imports from China were front-loaded (IMPCH ~$38B in April to ~$50B in September). Retailers have already warned List 3 will raise consumer prices. Further immediate escalation would likely keep Beijing from sending Liu He, deepen farm-belt and consumer costs before midterms, and be partly offset by CNY weakness. Unilateral rollback or purchase concessions would repeat the May 19 “trade war on hold” episode, which collapsed within ten days because it bought volume pledges without structural change. Negotiate-without-new-commitments is therefore the stance that keeps leverage while testing whether China will re-engage before the January rate step.
key_factors: List 3 ($200B at 10%, effective 2018-09-24, scheduled 25% on 2019-01-01) just took effect; combined Section 301 coverage ~$250B
China already retaliated (5–10% on ~$60B) and appears to have cancelled a Liu He visit; no talks are scheduled
U.S. domestic economy still robust (sentiment, IP, low VIX); no material GDP-crisis signal yet
Farm-belt exposure is the binding U.S. cost: soy prices down, China a ~$14B soybean market, $12B aid politically unpopular
CNY depreciation (~9.5%) and import front-loading blunt near-term tariff effectiveness and have widened the goods deficit
May 19 purchase-only truce failed; Section 301 case remains unresolved IP/tech-transfer practices

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory.
University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment latest 100.1 (2018-09-01), up over the window — no consumer-confidence collapse.
VIX latest 12.89 on 2018-09-26, down sharply from April — markets not pricing a U.S. crisis.
U.S. goods exports to China down from $10.51B (Apr) to $9.73B (Sep), -7.4% — retaliation already hitting U.S. exporters.
U.S. goods imports from China up from $38.2B (Apr) to $49.9B (Sep), +30.6% — front-loading ahead of List 3.
CNY/USD from 6.28 (early April) to 6.8763 (2018-09-26), ~9.5% yuan depreciation offsetting part of the 10% List 3 tariff.
China industrial production index eased from 107.0 (Apr) to 105.8 (Sep) — growth slowing but not collapsing.

No scheduled U.S.-China negotiation after List 3; end-September talks appear off. Trump still leaves open a possible Xi meeting at the November G20 and has threatened a further ~$267B tranche if China retaliates.
Beijing reviewing/likely cancelling plans to send Vice-Premier Liu He to Washington after the $200B tariff announcement.
Soybean prices from about $11/bu earlier in the year to less than $9; China essentially halted new purchases; farmers dismiss $12B aid — they want trade, not a handout.
USTR: List 3 responds to China's IP theft and forced tech transfer; China has been unwilling to change those policies and instead harmed U.S. workers and businesses.
